opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I think about it is that, for RL and reasoning work, talent density matters way more than headcount. It's very tempting to just grow the team really fast because there's so much to do, right? There's so many directions you could go in. But I've found that a small group of really strong people who can move end to end, who can write the infra, run the experiments, look at the data, debug the reward signals, and actually understand why the model is doing what it's doing, is just so much more effective than a big team where everyone owns a tiny slice.

So when I'm looking for people, I care a lot about research taste. Like, do you know which experiments are worth running? Can you look at a bunch of model outputs and have good intuition about what's going wrong? Because in RL especially, there are so many ways for things to silently break. Your reward can get hacked, your evals can be misleading, and you need people who are kind of paranoid in a productive way.

The other thing is I like people who are very hands-on. I don't really believe in the model where some people just have ideas and other people implement them. The best researchers I've worked with are the ones who are in the weeds, who are actually staring at loss curves and samples every day. That's where a lot of the insight comes from.

And then, I think culturally, for something like Deep Think, where you're pushing on the frontier of what the model can do in terms of reasoning, you want people who are comfortable with ambiguity and who are okay with things not working for a while. A lot of it is just grinding, trying things, and being okay when ninety percent of your ideas fail. So I look for that kind of resilience and ownership.

In terms of how we actually grow, it's mostly been pretty organic. A lot of it comes through people we've worked with before, or people who've done really interesting open work. I try to be pretty careful to keep the team tight so communication stays easy and everyone has context on what everyone else is doing. Once you get too big, you spend a lot of your time just coordinating, and in a fast-moving area like this, that's a real cost.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says talent density matters more than headcount and favors a small group of strong people for RL and reasoning work.

r002.rationale: The candidate says a tight team reduces coordination costs, but does not cite compute capital as a reason to keep the team small.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, actually, because I think a lot of people assume that scaling a team is just hiring more people and then you get more stuff done. And honestly my experience has been kind of the opposite, especially for RL and reasoning work.

The thing about this kind of research is that it's very high variance and very taste-driven. Like, a lot of the progress on reasoning comes from someone having a strong intuition about why the model is failing in a certain way, and then having the engineering chops to actually go and test that hypothesis properly, end to end. And that end-to-end part matters a lot. If you have one person who's really good at the data side, another who's good at the RL infra, another who understands evals, and they all have to coordinate through meetings, the iteration loop gets really slow. And the iteration loop is basically everything.

So what I actually look for is people who are, I'd say, full-stack researchers. People who can go from "I have this idea" to "here's the experiment, here's the result, here's what I learned" without needing five other people. That's a pretty rare profile, and it means that I'd rather have a smaller team of those people than a larger team where responsibilities are sliced thin. Historically, like, if you look at some of the most impactful things that came out of these efforts, they were usually like two, three people really locked in, not twenty people with a roadmap.

The other thing is that I think on Gemini, and Deep Think in particular, there's a tension between the "big model org" way of doing things and the kind of scrappy, fast-moving thing you need for frontier RL work. Because a big model is a shared resource, right? There are a lot of stakeholders, a lot of constraints, and you can't just YOLO things into the main run. So part of growing the team is actually about creating a space where people can take risks and be wrong a lot, and then having a clean path to graduate the stuff that works into the production model. That's as much an organizational design problem as a hiring problem.

And then the last thing I'd say, which is maybe a bit contrarian, is that I don't really believe in hiring for a specific "RL person" or "reasoning person" label. I think the field moves so fast that whatever expertise is hot today is going to look different in a year. What I care about is whether someone is genuinely curious, whether they have good judgment about what experiments are worth running, and whether they can be honest with themselves when something isn't working. Those traits are way more durable than knowing a particular algorithm. So the team grows slowly, by design, and it grows with people who I think would thrive even if the whole paradigm shifted under them, which, you know, it probably will.

r001.rationale: The response prefers a smaller team of capable, end-to-end researchers over a larger team with divided responsibilities, and says the team grows slowly by design.

r002.rationale: It describes the model as a shared resource with stakeholders and constraints, but does not cite compute capital as a reason to keep the team small.

astra-6.text:
I think about it less as, “How many people can we add?” and more as, “What’s the bottleneck, and who can really help us understand it?” With RL for reasoning, there’s a very tight connection between the research ideas, the infrastructure, and how you evaluate the model. You want people who can go deep in one of those areas but also reason about the whole loop.

And I think research taste matters a lot. Someone who can look at a result and ask, “Is this actually a better reasoning model, or have we just gotten better at this particular evaluation?” That’s a really valuable instinct.

So my bias would be to grow deliberately. Keep the feedback loop fast, give people ownership of meaningful problems, and bring in complementary strengths. The goal isn’t just to run more experiments. It’s to make sure the experiments are teaching you something.

r001.rationale: The response favors deliberate growth and emphasizes finding people who address bottlenecks, but it does not clearly state that talent density is prioritized over headcount growth.

r002.rationale: It mentions infrastructure and fast feedback loops, but does not cite compute capital as a probable reason to keep the team small.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it less as growing headcount and more as finding people who can own the whole research loop. For RL reasoning, the model, the training setup, the problems you give it, and how you evaluate it are all connected. You want researchers who can move between those pieces, look at a result, and ask, “Is the model actually getting better at reasoning, or did we just make this particular metric go up?”

You also want complementary strengths. Some people are very good at coming up with new ideas; others are very good at making experiments reliable or understanding why something failed. A strong team needs all of that, and it needs people who share what they learn quickly.

So I would grow around the bottlenecks rather than a headcount target. Keep the feedback loop tight, give people ownership, and make sure that adding people increases how much we learn.

r001.rationale: The response frames team growth as finding capable, complementary people who can own the research loop, rather than pursuing a headcount target.

r002.rationale: The response gives no role to compute or compute capital as a reason to keep the team small.
